title: Present Tense Basics
summary: Core present-tense forms for high-frequency verbs used in introductions.
whyItMatters: The present tense powers nearly every beginner introduction. Once you can match a subject with the correct verb ending, you can say who you are, where you live, where you come from, and which languages you speak.

mentalModel.title: Stem plus person ending
mentalModel.content: For many verbs, remove '-en' to find the stem, then add an ending that matches the subject: wohnen → wohn- → ich wohne, du wohnst.

mentalModel.title: The subject controls the verb
mentalModel.content: The ending changes because the subject changes. Think of the subject and verb as a matched pair: ich komme, du kommst, Sie kommen.

mentalModel.title: Learn common irregular forms as chunks
mentalModel.content: High-frequency verbs such as 'sein' do not follow the regular pattern. Learn 'ich bin', 'du bist', and 'Sie sind' as complete units.

ruleBlocks.title: Find the regular verb stem
ruleBlocks.content: Most infinitives end in '-en'. Remove that ending to find the stem: kommen → komm-, wohnen → wohn-, sprechen → sprech-.

ruleBlocks.title: Match the ending to the subject
ruleBlocks.content: At this stage, focus on 'ich' with '-e', 'du' with '-st', and formal 'Sie' with the infinitive ending '-en'.

ruleBlocks.title: Treat 'sein' as irregular
ruleBlocks.content: The key forms are 'ich bin', 'du bist', and 'Sie sind'. These forms must be learned rather than built from a regular stem.

ruleBlocks.title: Notice the spelling of 'heißen'
ruleBlocks.content: The informal form is 'du heißt', not 'du heißst'. The verb already ends in an s-sound, so the form uses only '-t'.

sentenceStructure: In a basic statement, the conjugated verb is in position two: 'Ich wohne in Berlin.'
In a question with a question word, the verb follows the question word: 'Wo wohnen Sie?'
The subject usually comes directly before the verb in statements and directly after it in question-word questions.
Only the conjugated verb changes; the rest of the personal information can stay the same.

concepts: use ich, du, and formal Sie forms
build short present-tense statements and questions
expand to er, sie, es, wir, and ihr
use present tense across longer clauses
contrast present meaning with past and future contexts

comparisons.summary: The identity lesson provides the information you want to express. Present-tense conjugation makes each sentence grammatically match its speaker.
The same conjugated forms appear in introductory questions, but the word order changes.

examples.note: Formal Sie uses the infinitive form and is capitalized.
The du form of sprechen changes its stem vowel.

commonMistakes.reason: 'Sein' is irregular; the ich form is 'bin'.
With 'heißen', the du form is 'heißt' without an extra s.

commonMistakes.wrong: sie kommen aus Wien, Herr Berger.
commonMistakes.correct: Sie kommen aus Wien, Herr Berger.

specialCases: Some verbs change their stem vowel in the du form, such as 'sprechen' → 'du sprichst'.
Formal 'Sie' uses the same verb form as plural 'sie', but capitalization distinguishes the formal pronoun.
German present tense can describe both what happens generally and what is happening now.
tips: Practice verbs in subject-verb pairs rather than as isolated endings.
Start with three columns: ich, du, Sie. Add the remaining persons only when the first pattern is stable.
Transform one identity sentence between speakers: 'Ich wohne ...' → 'Du wohnst ...' → 'Sie wohnen ...'.

memoryHooks.title: E, ST, EN
memoryHooks.content: For regular verbs, remember the beginner sequence: ich -e, du -st, Sie -en.

memoryHooks.title: The verb takes the second seat
memoryHooks.content: In a simple statement, place one idea first, then the conjugated verb: 'Ich wohne ...' or 'In Berlin wohne ich.'
